title: Choosing quilter's cotton for embroidery
subtitle: When quilter's cotton suits embroidery and how to pick it.
excerpt: Quilter's cotton is a closely woven, even-weave cotton with a slightly smooth hand. It holds a crease, takes transfer marks cleanly, and suits most surface embroidery techniques. This reading explains what to look for and what to avoid.
sourceNotes: Fabric selection principles consistent with contemporary needlework practice. No single public-domain source; synthesised from standard embroidery teaching.

glossaryTerms.definition: A tightly woven, medium-weight plain-weave cotton fabric with a smooth surface and low stretch. Originally intended for patchwork and quilting, but its even weave and firm hand also suit surface embroidery.

content.text: is one of the most reliable fabrics for beginners starting surface embroidery. It is easy to source, comes in hundreds of colours and prints, and behaves predictably under the needle.

Quilter's cotton has a tight, even weave that sits steady in the hoop. It accepts water-soluble pen marks cleanly and the marks wash out fully. The thread count is consistent, so stitches sit level. It also creases well, which means the design area stays flat while you work.
What to look for when choosing

Look for a thread count of 60 to 80 threads per 2.5 cm. Lower counts have visible gaps between threads and stitches sink into them. Hold the fabric up to the light. A tight, consistent weave shows a fine, even grid. Loosely woven cloth shows open spaces.

Avoid quilter's cottons with a glossy finish or a stiff hand. Some are treated with sizing to make them easier to cut in quilting; this sizing washes out and can leave the fabric limp. Pre-wash the fabric before embroidering if you plan to wash the finished piece.

For counted thread work such as cross stitch, choose Aida or evenweave linen rather than quilter's cotton. The irregular weave of quilter's cotton makes counting difficult. For goldwork or heavy metal thread work, the fabric needs to be mounted on a heavier ground cloth (a linen twill or wool felt) rather than used alone.
